newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street stocks, dollar little changed on Deng death.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street stocks, dollar little changed on Deng death.

text.p: Wall Street stocks held to narrow ranges in quiet afternoon trading Wednesday as the market showed little response to news of the death of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping.
The dollar briefly jumped higher, but then gave up the gain.

"I think in the West, Deng was largely viewed as a figurehead, so I wouldn't expect much reaction," said Michael Metz, chief investment strategist at Oppenheimer and Co. "It's really been several years since he faded to the background and the power there has already been passed on to others."

U.S.-listed shares in China-related funds also showed little reaction to the news. Templeton China World Fund Inc. dipped 1/4 to 12-7/8 and Jardine Fleming China Region Fund Inc. was unchanged at 11-5/8.

The Dow Jones industrial average was up about 3 points at 7,070 and the S&P 500 index fell fractionally to 816 shortly after 2 p.m. EST. Advancing and declining issues were about even on volume of about 360 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The dollar briefly spiked higher against the mark and rose to session highs against the yen on news of the death of China's paramount leader, dealers said.
However, the knee-jerk rise was short-lived, and traders in New York said they expected little further price action on the news, which was widely anticipated.
"They were buying dollars and dollar/mark popped up past a resistance level at 1.70 marks, but it has come off since," said Doug Lee, assistant vice president at Sakura Bank Ltd.

The Hong Kong dollar and the Thai bhat fell initially, said John Nelson, foreign exchange trading manager at ABN-AMRO Bank. He added that it could take some time for market players to calculate the long-term impact on the regional currencies.

"I don't think it has any implications for U.S. or European markets. Even in the case of Pacific Rim markets, this news has been largely discounted over the last several years," said John Williams, managing director and chief global markets economist at Bankers Trust.
